results.title: Why we built Continual-ARC. · unify
results.content:
A harness could still prove us wrong, most likely one that refactors what it keeps into small functions it can reuse. Re-ARC writes all 400 training rules from one library of 160 primitive functions, and program synthesis has learned libraries like that before[\[15\]](#ref-15)[\[19\]](#ref-19).

## What carries over to real harnesses

Office work has no task ids to file programs by, but we think three lessons from ARC still hold for any harness.

- Store liberally, the examples paid for included, and prune later.
- Store functions, not just notes, checked against the examples kept.
- Bring back what's stored without being asked, by what the current work looks like, which OpenClaw didn't. [...] On this stream, though, only training made the model better at puzzles it hadn't seen. For an agent in deployment, we'd train the model that drives the harness as well as give it a memory.

## Limitations and what's next

The stream comes from ARC-AGI-1's public training set, which every model developer knows, and a model may know some of these rules already. Notes and weights are compared on one open student, with one teacher and one seed. None of our models is the strongest available, and a stronger one might keep notes that answer a returning puzzle. Next is Drift, in which a puzzle's rule changes quietly partway through the stream and what a learner keeps can go stale. [...] ## Only the weights got better at new puzzles

On Qwen's held-out test, no version that keeps notes saved more than 0.03, and the program library, which can't carry anything to a puzzle it hasn't met, saved nothing measurable. Trained to imitate GLM, Qwen saved 0.29 of what the untrained model spent there, solving about 49 of the 100 new puzzles to the untrained model's 19, and 31 for the same model with no harness at all.

results.title: Paper page - Continual-ARC: Measuring Skill Acquisition over a Working Lifetime
results.content:
Agent harnesses have emerged as a promising mechanism for continual learning, alongside test-time parametric learning. However, the current benchmarks have several limitations: they generally focus on a single applied domain, serve each instance only once, and assume a single family of learner, so memory-based and weight-based systems are rarely compared on the same scale. We propose Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream built from the three ARC-AGI editions, whose tasks need no domain knowledge. The same tasks return after dormant gaps with fresh instances, while new tasks keep arriving. On each instance, the learner may pay for demonstrations, submit answers, or act inside the harness, with retries permitted on incorrect submissions, which are paid for. Each instance is scored based on the [...] Out of the box, most harnesses didn't learn measurably, and most of the harness-based methods we tried learned less than a baseline that just caches each task's demonstrations. Told explicitly to save a verified program per task, all three harnesses we ran on GPT-6 Luna memorized, but they gained little or nothing on unseen tasks. Training the weights did generalize: Qwen3.5-9B, trained with DAgger to imitate GLM-5.3 Flash, spent 29% less than its untrained self on the 100 unseen tasks.

Caveat: it's one domain, and most of our runs use fairly small models. Would love to hear where you think the benchmark falls short! [...] Hugging Face's logo

# Continual-ARC: Measuring Skill Acquisition over a Working Lifetime

unifyai

## Abstract

Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-AGI tasks, compares memory- and weight-based continual learning under frozen-weight agent harnesses, revealing that harness persistence rarely improves memorization and most harness methods underperform simple caching, while weight-based learning shows better generalization.
